paragraphs: The paper connects two problems: learning how to measure distances between examples and finding a lower-dimensional representation of data. It proposes a transductive framework for distance metric learning and explains its close relationship with several nonlinear spectral dimensionality reduction methods. This gives the two tasks a shared mathematical treatment.

The authors also prove a representer theorem that connects the framework to estimating functions in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, or RKHS. This connection matters because it makes generalization to previously unseen samples possible. The framework therefore has a route beyond representing only the samples used to construct its initial solution.

Computationally, the framework requires solving a sparse eigenvalue problem. The abstract reports that this permits handling datasets of around one hundred thousand samples. Experiments cover synthetic data, UCI datasets, and handwritten digits from MNIST. Together, the theoretical connection and computational formulation offer a way to study distance learning through established spectral methods.
icml-2007-a-transductive-framework-of-di.tldr: A spectral framework connects distance metric learning with nonlinear dimensionality reduction and provides a route to generalizing beyond the observed samples.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to compress large three-dimensional meshes using the connections between their vertices. Spectral compression represents an object's geometry using basis functions derived from its graph Laplacian. Computing these functions reliably becomes numerically challenging when an object contains more than one hundred thousand vertices, motivating a different representation.

The proposed method uses diffusion wavelets, which extend wavelets to graphs with arbitrary connectivity. Their basis functions are compact and operate at multiple scales, unlike the global Laplacian bases discussed in the paper. This gives the compression method a representation organized around local structure at different levels of detail.

To work with large meshes, the authors partition the graph using a fast method, compute local multiscale bases on the resulting subgraphs, and combine them. Their reported results show that diffusion wavelet bases outperform Laplacian bases for adaptive compression of large three-dimensional objects. The contribution combines a different kind of representation with a strategy for constructing it on large graphs.
icml-2007-adaptive-mesh-compression-in-3.tldr: Local, multiscale diffusion wavelet bases improve adaptive compression of large 3D meshes in the reported comparisons with Laplacian bases.

paragraphs: The paper examines how to generate the basis functions used to approximate a value function in reinforcement learning. These functions provide the building blocks of the approximation. Rather than treating their choice as separate from the approximation problem, the analyzed approach uses Bellman error to guide the construction of additional building blocks.

The authors establish two linked properties of this approach. It generates orthogonal basis functions, giving the representation mathematically distinct directions. It also provably tightens bounds on approximation error. The second result supplies a theoretical reason to use the generated features: their addition improves the stated bounds on how well the value function can be approximated.

The paper also illustrates the approach on sample problems containing noise. These examples address its use when the available information is imperfect, alongside the theoretical analysis. The central contribution is a connection between an error-based feature-generation rule and stronger approximation bounds, rather than simply a demonstration that adding more features can change a learned value function.
icml-2007-analyzing-feature-generation-f.tldr: A Bellman-error-based feature-generation method produces orthogonal basis functions and provably tightens value-function approximation error bounds.

paragraphs: Asymmetric boosting addresses classification problems in which different kinds of mistakes carry different costs. The paper derives a cost-sensitive boosting method from decision theory and the statistical interpretation of boosting. Its central step is to incorporate those costs into a principled loss function, giving the learning objective an explicit connection to the consequences of errors.

The algorithm minimizes this loss through gradient descent over convex combinations of weak learners, following the general approach used by AdaBoost. It also produces large-margin detectors. When the costs of errors are equal, the method reduces to AdaBoost, so ordinary boosting appears as a special case of the same formulation.

Experiments provide evidence for both cost sensitivity and large margins. In face detection, the method outperforms several earlier heuristic approaches to cost-sensitive boosting. These findings support the practical value of deriving the loss from decision-theoretic principles in the evaluated setting, while the equal-cost connection explains how the method relates to an established boosting algorithm.
icml-2007-asymmetric-boosting-6efbd01881.tldr: Asymmetric boosting derives a cost-sensitive loss from decision theory, reduces to AdaBoost for equal error costs, and improves face detection in reported comparisons.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether a reinforcement learning system can automatically restructure its reward signal to learn faster. It first introduces a method for learning a shaped reward function when state abstractions and temporal abstractions are supplied. The aim is to make the rewards used during learning more helpful for acquiring behavior.

The authors then consider agents made of multiple units that act concurrently on different tasks. In these settings, the reward at each time step can be decomposed among the units. An example shows that finding a good decomposition can require shaping the reward first, making the two design problems closely connected.

A function approximation algorithm addresses shaping and decomposition together. This matters because a reward structure suitable for the whole agent may need adjustment before it becomes useful for its separate units. The proposed methods can augment standard reinforcement learning algorithms, and the reported experiments show significantly faster learning in each tested case. The empirical result supports learning the reward organization as part of the learning process.
icml-2007-automatic-shaping-and-decompos.tldr: Learning reward shaping and reward decomposition together speeds up standard reinforcement learning algorithms in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Markov logic networks combine weighted logical clauses with probabilistic modeling. Learning their structure means deciding which clauses should be included. The paper examines a weakness of an existing top-down method: it systematically generates many candidate structures before considering the data, then greedily searches according to how well those candidates fit.

Such a search can get stuck at local maxima or plateaus. The proposed bottom-up approach instead uses a propositional Markov network learning method to construct template networks. Those templates guide the creation of candidate clauses, allowing information learned from the data to influence which logical structures are considered.

The authors report significantly improved accuracy and learning time over the existing top-down approach in three real-world domains. These results support changing the way candidates are constructed, as well as evaluating their statistical fit. The contribution is a data-guided route into the structure search, with empirical evidence that this route can produce better models more quickly in the studied domains.
icml-2007-bottom-up-learning-of-markov-l.tldr: Data-derived template networks guide bottom-up Markov logic structure learning, improving accuracy and learning time in three real-world domains.

paragraphs: The paper compares several approaches to structured learning, including sequence labeling. These problems require predicting related outputs together, so the choice of model concerns how an entire output structure is learned. The comparison includes hidden Markov models, conditional random fields, averaged perceptrons, structured support vector machines, max-margin Markov networks, and SEARN.

The authors make parameter-tuning efforts for each model before comparing results. On the datasets they evaluate, structured support vector machines perform better than the other individual methods. This is a result about the tested datasets and tuning process; its value is a comparative assessment across several prominent approaches under that evaluation.

The paper also introduces a Structured Learning Ensemble that combines the structured learning models. Empirically, this ensemble provides more accurate solutions than the best individual model results. The two contributions therefore answer related questions: which individual method performs best in the study, and whether combining methods can improve on choosing that single winner.
icml-2007-comparisons-of-sequence-labeli.tldr: Structured SVMs lead the evaluated individual models, while a proposed ensemble achieves still higher accuracy in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: This paper studies what kernel principal component analysis does when used before supervised learning. Dimensionality reduction changes the representation passed to a predictor, but the authors focus on its regularization effect: how retaining only part of a representation controls the learning procedure. They analyze a specific combination of projection and regression.

That combination first applies kernel principal component analysis and then fits ordinary least squares to the projected data. The resulting method, kernel principal component regression, is shown to be equivalent to spectral cut-off regularization. The number of retained principal components is exactly the regularization parameter, directly connecting representation size to the mathematical form of regularization.

Using probabilistic estimates for integral operators, the authors derive error estimates for the method. They also propose a procedure for choosing the parameter that allows them to prove consistency. This supplies a theoretical basis for selecting how many components to keep, connecting a preprocessing decision with the generalization properties of the resulting regression algorithm.
icml-2007-dimensionality-reduction-and-g.tldr: Kernel principal component regression is spectral cut-off regularization, with the retained component count controlling regularization and enabling consistency analysis.

paragraphs: The paper develops discriminant learning around correlation, a widely used way to measure similarity. Its motivation is that much discriminant learning work has focused on distance measures, while correlation has received comparatively little attention. The proposed Correlation Discriminant Analysis method makes correlation the basis for learning a transformation of the data.

The method defines correlation within classes and between classes. It then seeks a transformation that maximizes the difference between these quantities. This gives the transformation a classification-oriented objective: the correlation relationships it creates should distinguish examples belonging to the same class from examples belonging to different classes.

The authors provide different implementations for different cases of the transformation. Their empirical evaluations show an advantage over alternative methods and associate the correlation objective with good classification performance. The finding supports correlation as a useful setting for discriminant learning in the evaluated problems, expanding the kinds of similarity relationships that a learned representation can explicitly optimize.
icml-2007-discriminant-analysis-in-corre.tldr: Correlation Discriminant Analysis learns transformations that separate within-class and between-class correlation, with empirical advantages over evaluated alternatives.

paragraphs: This paper addresses learning relationships from pairs of natural language sentences. Its proposed family of syntactic kernels gives a learning algorithm a way to use sentence structure when working with those pairs. The focus on paired sentences makes the representation relevant to tasks in which the relationship between texts is the object of prediction.

The computational contribution is an optimized dynamic programming algorithm for evaluating the kernels. Kernel evaluation is part of using these models, so making it efficient matters alongside defining a useful structural comparison. The paper therefore treats the representation and the procedure for computing it as connected parts of the approach.

The authors evaluate the kernels with support vector machines on textual entailment recognition and question answering. They report both effectiveness and efficiency on these tasks. The results support using syntactic kernels for these two forms of relational text learning, while the optimized evaluation procedure addresses the computational work needed to put that representation into use.
icml-2007-fast-and-effective-kernels-for.tldr: Optimized syntactic kernels support effective and efficient sentence-pair learning for textual entailment and question answering.

paragraphs: The paper studies retrieval from structured data collections when queries contain noise. A useful retrieval system must identify appropriate matches, but growing collections also make search efficiency important. The authors address both concerns by learning a similarity function with the retrieval data structure explicitly in mind.

Their algorithm uses functional gradient boosting to optimize retrieval accuracy together with the efficiency of vantage point trees. The learned similarity function therefore influences both which items count as good matches and how effectively the search structure retrieves them. This connects the statistical goal of accurate matching with the computational goal of carrying out retrieval efficiently.

The approach is demonstrated on two datasets, including a moderately sized real-world collection of folk music. The reported effectiveness supports treating similarity learning and retrieval efficiency as a joint problem in these settings. Its central contribution is an objective that considers how a learned comparison will be used by the search system, alongside its ability to tolerate noisy queries.
icml-2007-learning-for-efficient-retriev.tldr: The paper learns similarity functions that jointly improve noisy-query retrieval accuracy and the efficiency of vantage point trees.

paragraphs: This paper learns representations for action-value functions, which assign values to choices made in particular states. Earlier work used Laplacian basis functions constructed from states. The proposed approach includes the agent's actions when constructing the representation, making the basis functions directly reflect the state-action setting of the approximation problem.

The authors obtain the basis functions through a spectral decomposition of a state-action manifold. This yields a learned nonlinear representation and avoids duplicating state bases across actions as in previous work. They discuss both off-policy and on-policy methods for building the state-action graphs on which the representation depends.

The paper reports greater expressive power and better performance than state-based Laplacian basis functions in domains modeled as semi-Markov decision processes. It also presents a simple graph partitioning method for scaling to large discrete Markov decision processes. Together, these contributions address what information the representation contains and how the graph-based construction can be made workable for larger problems.
icml-2007-learning-state-action-basis-fu.tldr: Spectral bases learned from state-action graphs improve action-value representations and outperform state-only Laplacian bases in the studied semi-Markov domains.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a probabilistic way to learn variation in shape contours from noisy observations. Its low-dimensional nonlinear latent variable model represents complex shape changes while explicitly accounting for noise. This addresses a weakness of approaches that optimize a data-space objective without a corresponding noise model.

A second contribution concerns how observed points are associated with the underlying contour. Many approaches move data points around fixed contours and need a correctly labeled reference shape to avoid degenerate solutions. Here, the observed points remain fixed while the unobserved curves are reparameterized to explain them. The paper states that the reference-shape problem consequently does not arise.

The algorithms can use arbitrary basis functions and apply to both open and closed shapes. Their effectiveness is demonstrated with illustrative examples, quantitative benchmark assessments, and a visualization task. These evaluations support a formulation that combines noise modeling with a different treatment of contour parameterization, allowing shape variation to be learned without the stated reference-shape requirement.
icml-2007-linear-and-nonlinear-generativ.tldr: A probabilistic latent-variable approach learns complex contour variation from noisy points while avoiding the stated need for a labeled reference shape.

paragraphs: The paper extends the pachinko allocation model to represent a nested hierarchy of topics. The earlier four-level model represents correlations among topics through a directed acyclic graph, but does not explicitly provide broader topics whose word distributions capture vocabulary shared by more specific topics. Hierarchical PAM adds that capability.

The resulting model combines a topical hierarchy with the ability to mix multiple leaves of that hierarchy. Broad and specific topics can therefore coexist in the representation, while a document can draw on multiple specific topics. This brings together the hierarchical organization associated with hLDA and the flexible topic mixing associated with PAM.

Experiments show improvements in the likelihood assigned to held-out documents and in mutual information between discovered topics and human-created categories, such as journals. These findings address two different aspects of the model: how well it accounts for unseen documents and how closely its learned topics relate to external categories. Both results support the added hierarchical representation in the reported evaluations.
icml-2007-mixtures-of-hierarchical-topic.tldr: Hierarchical PAM combines nested topics with flexible topic mixtures, improving held-out likelihood and alignment with human categories in experiments.

paragraphs: The paper studies multi-armed bandits whose choices are statistically related. It assumes that these dependencies are described by a generative model over clusters of arms. This structure gives the decision policy information about relationships among choices, creating an opportunity to improve on methods designed for independent arms.

For discounted rewards, the authors identify an optimal policy based on a Markov decision process and provide an approximation with a formal error guarantee. For undiscounted rewards, they discuss lower bounds on regret and propose a general two-level bandit policy. These separate treatments address different ways of evaluating reward over time.

The paper develops three versions of the two-level policy and theoretically explains how their regret depends on cluster characteristics. Experiments on large-scale real-world and synthetic data show significant improvements over classical independent-arm policies. The contribution links the usefulness of dependency information to both policy design and theoretical analysis, with empirical support under the studied clustered-arm settings.
icml-2007-multi-armed-bandit-problems-wi.tldr: Policies that exploit modeled dependencies within arm clusters gain theoretical support and outperform independent-arm bandit policies in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a Bayesian framework for learning several related sequential-data tasks together. Standard hidden Markov models often require choosing the number of hidden states before learning. The authors instead assign each task an infinite hidden Markov model, avoiding that advance choice of a fixed state count.

To connect the tasks, the framework places a nested Dirichlet process prior on the base distributions of their models. This allows clustering at two levels simultaneously: among tasks and within their data. The shared hierarchy supports learning individual sequence models while also discovering similarities between tasks.

Learning and inference use a Gibbs sampler. The framework is demonstrated on synthetic sequences and real music data. Its significance is the joint treatment of model structure and relationships across tasks: the method can learn how tasks group together while fitting their sequential patterns. The reported demonstrations support the effectiveness of this combined nonparametric approach for the data considered.
icml-2007-multi-task-learning-for-sequen.tldr: A nested Dirichlet process connects infinite HMMs to learn sequential tasks jointly while discovering task similarities and data clusters.

paragraphs: The paper asks how to discover a manifold that preserves information useful for nonlinear regression. This brings prediction into dimensionality reduction: the desired representation should retain what matters for the regression problem. The authors connect sufficient dimension reduction, traditionally focused on linear subspaces, with manifold learning, traditionally focused on unsupervised representations.

Their method combines kernel dimension reduction with Laplacian eigenmaps. More specifically, it optimizes cross-covariance operators in kernel feature spaces constructed from the normalized graph Laplacian. This mathematical combination makes the learned manifold sensitive to the supervised regression objective, extending the representation beyond the linear-subspace setting.

The approach is described as flexible because it makes no strong assumptions about either the regression function or the distribution of the input variables. The authors illustrate it using global temperature data and image manifolds. These applications demonstrate the methodology's use in finding representations organized around predictive information, bringing the geometry of the data and the needs of regression into one procedure.
icml-2007-regression-on-manifolds-using-.tldr: Combining kernel dimension reduction with Laplacian eigenmaps yields supervised manifolds designed to preserve information relevant to nonlinear regression.

paragraphs: The paper addresses robot control problems that can be reformulated as immediate-reward reinforcement learning, including operational space control. Online robot learning places practical demands on optimization: updates must be efficient, scale to complex robots, and avoid requiring trials of policies generated through infeasible random searches on a physical system.

The authors generalize an expectation-maximization-based reinforcement learning framework to reduce immediate-reward learning to reward-weighted regression. This reformulation makes regression the central learning operation. It also incorporates an adaptive reward transformation intended to accelerate convergence, treating the handling of rewards as an integrated part of the algorithm.

The resulting method is reported to be efficient, to learn smoothly without dangerous jumps in solution space, and to work well on complex robots with many degrees of freedom. These claims address the computational and behavioral requirements motivating the work. The contribution applies to the stated immediate-reward formulation, showing how that structure can support a practical learning procedure for demanding robot-control applications.
icml-2007-reinforcement-learning-by-rewa.tldr: Reward-weighted regression with an adaptive reward transformation provides efficient, smooth learning for robot-control problems formulated with immediate rewards.

paragraphs: The paper considers clustering when the available data describe only pairwise similarities or dissimilarities between objects. Such relations are stored in a matrix, and separate descriptions of the objects may be unavailable. Although graph partitioning can express some relational clustering problems, the authors argue that it is inadequate as a general formulation.

They propose symmetric convex coding as a general model for relational clustering. The model is presented as applicable to all types of relational data and as unifying the existing graph partitioning formulation. This places graph-based clustering within a broader framework for working directly with relation matrices.

The authors derive two alternative bound-optimization algorithms, using Euclidean distance and generalized I-divergence respectively. These provide concrete procedures for solving the coding problem under two different distance functions. Experimental evaluation and theoretical analysis support the effectiveness and potential of the model and algorithms. The contribution therefore joins a general formulation with optimization methods for learning clusters from pairwise information.
icml-2007-relational-clustering-by-symme.tldr: Symmetric convex coding provides a general relational clustering framework that includes graph partitioning and supports two bound-optimization algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper examines probabilistic clustering methods that use constraints between pairs of data points. Its focus is what happens when some supplied constraints are incorrect. Such information is intended to guide clustering, but the evaluation shows that the way a method handles constraints strongly affects its robustness to mistakes.

The chunklet model strictly enforces the supplied constraints. The authors find that it can produce poor results even when only a small number are misspecified. Methods that penalize violations are more robust to incorrect constraints, but the analysis identifies undesirable local behaviors in those approaches as well.

Motivated by these findings, the paper extends the chunklet model to accept soft constraints expressed through an intuitive confidence measure. This gives the learning method a way to represent uncertainty about the guidance it receives. The contribution combines an assessment of existing failure modes with a revised formulation in which a pairwise constraint need not be treated as completely certain.
icml-2007-revisiting-probabilistic-model.tldr: After identifying weaknesses in hard and penalized clustering constraints, the paper extends the chunklet model with confidence-based soft constraints.

paragraphs: Expectation regularization is a semi-supervised method designed to make unlabeled data useful within exponential-family parametric models. The paper is motivated by practical obstacles to deploying semi-supervised learning, including difficult implementation, fragile tuning, and limited scalability. It introduces an additional training signal that can be combined with the usual labeled-data objective.

Specifically, the method augments conditional label likelihood with a term encouraging predictions on unlabeled examples to match specified expectations. Label priors are one example of such expectations. This lets information about expected predictions influence learning even when individual examples do not have labels, alongside the direct supervision available from labeled data.

The authors describe the method as very easy to implement, report scalability comparable to logistic regression, and state that it can handle non-independent features. Experiments on five datasets show accuracy improvements over other semi-supervised methods. These results support a practical way to incorporate expectations into training, connecting a simple objective modification with gains in the evaluated tasks.
icml-2007-simple-robust-scalable-semi-su.tldr: Expectation regularization uses expected predictions on unlabeled data to improve semi-supervised learning while retaining logistic-regression-like scalability.

paragraphs: The paper proposes three probabilistic language models that predict the next word from several preceding words. Their motivation is data sparsity, a challenge for language modeling that distributed word representations can help address. The models use real-valued representations of words as part of the mechanism for predicting the next-word distribution.

These representations are learned jointly with a large set of stochastic binary hidden features. The hidden features are used to predict the next word's distributed representation from those of previous words. Learning both components together links the word representation to the predictive structure of the language model.

The authors find that connecting the binary hidden features to their previous states improves performance. Direct connections between real-valued word representations also help. One of the three models significantly outperforms the strongest n-gram models in the reported comparison. The findings support both the distributed-representation approach and particular connection patterns within these graphical models, rather than attributing the same result to all three variants.
icml-2007-three-new-graphical-models-for.tldr: Three language models jointly learn word representations and stochastic hidden features, with one significantly outperforming the best n-gram models in the reported comparison.

paragraphs: The paper addresses learning speed when reinforcement learning uses piecewise linear value-function approximation. It starts from a broader difficulty: combining reinforcement learning with linear approximation can cause instability. Methods that minimize mean-square Bellman error offer convergence guarantees, but may learn slowly or require expensive computation.

The proposed approach tracks changes in the value function using a Kalman filter and a random-walk model. This treats the evolving value function as something to estimate dynamically during learning. The random-walk model is the stated modeling choice underlying that tracking procedure, and the intended benefit is faster convergence of the approximation.

The authors present the approach as a general framework and implement TD, Q-learning, and MAXQ within it for different domains. Their empirical results demonstrate improved learning speed over previous methods. These findings support value-function tracking as a way to accelerate the evaluated algorithms; the abstract's convergence guarantees concern the Bellman-error-minimizing methods discussed as background, rather than establishing a new universal guarantee for the proposed framework.
icml-2007-tracking-value-function-dynami.tldr: Kalman-filter tracking of value-function dynamics improves learning speed for piecewise linear TD, Q-learning, and MAXQ implementations in reported experiments.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to train logistic regression efficiently on large problems, with document classification and natural language processing as motivating applications. The statistical objective remains maximizing the model's log likelihood. The contribution concerns the numerical method used to reach that objective when training involves large amounts of data.

The authors apply a trust region Newton method. Its stated strategy uses approximate Newton steps early in optimization while achieving fast convergence near the end. This division matters because the method does not require the same degree of step accuracy throughout training; its early behavior and final convergence are designed to serve different stages of the optimization.

Experiments show that the proposed method runs faster than the commonly used quasi-Newton approach to logistic regression. The paper also compares it with linear support vector machine implementations. The stated speed advantage concerns the logistic-regression optimizer comparison, offering empirical evidence that changing the optimization method can make this established model more practical at large scale.
icml-2007-trust-region-newton-methods-fo.tldr: A trust region Newton method trains large-scale logistic regression faster than a commonly used quasi-Newton approach in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: A noisy-channel model describes how an original message becomes corrupted and how it might be reconstructed. It separates a language model of the original message from a channel model of the corruption process. The paper focuses on learning the channel parameters without supervision, a task commonly approached by maximizing the likelihood of observed data.

The standard estimation procedure usually uses expectation-maximization, or EM. The authors instead propose maximizing the joint likelihood of data at both ends of the channel and derive a corresponding bidirectional EM algorithm. This changes the estimation objective so that learning accounts for the two ends together.

The method is evaluated on translation with a probabilistic lexicon and on adapting a part-of-speech tagger between related languages. In both tasks, the bidirectional procedure performs better than standard EM. These findings support the proposed joint-likelihood objective for the evaluated applications and show that changing how a noisy-channel model is estimated can improve its usefulness in language-processing tasks.
icml-2007-unsupervised-estimation-for-no.tldr: Bidirectional EM learns noisy-channel models using joint likelihood at both ends and improves on standard EM in two language-processing tasks.
